reply_sources.native_exact_quote:
Oops, Thanks, indeed I should add definition on that part.

Weakly expressive is like "音符和时间信息已经存在，但目标力度层被简化，例如 MIDI velocity 全部设为默认值，无法保留逐音力度变化 (set to 64, or 8-labels scale quantization.)"

Weak supervise is the missing of groundtruth labels, or low quality groundtruth.

actual_reply_item_table.reviewer_comment_exact: Table 1.2: would a scenario of converting performance audio to MIDI velocity also apply, particularly for the work done in chapter 6?
actual_reply_item_table.relevant_exact_excerpt: but we have not yet established.
actual_reply_item_table.assessment_zh: 解释目前采用S2；audio-only适配尚未建立，不是整项NO或承诺改表。

reply_sources.native_exact_quote: At current, I am success in Senario 2. We use a score-informed MIDI velocity estimation model because it performs better and provides a stronger pre-train model for adaptation.Normal MIDI velocity estimation, those without music score as prior, for example the hFT Transformer by Toyama ISMIR2023 is about 3 times MAE than our baseline system. So adapt these audio-only (S3) model with DDSP or DIff-SFProxy is good problem to explore, but we have not yet established.Current method is useful, As we demonstrated in Chapter 4, the audio–score misalignments won't affect much. So it works well.So it's good to explore border application. I believe.

actual_reply_item_table.reviewer_comment_exact: Figure 2.1: does there need to be always a correspondence between the Perceptual level and the MIDI velocity level? Could there be a direct link between the Perceptual level to the Score Dynamics level?

reply_sources.native_exact_quote:
Ture, but and False. This correspondence is about the instrument-specific tones, and Performer style. Like two different piano will give different sound with the same finger force. And, about the skill, this could said the piano pedal, and many other factor influence it. So it's false, because too many uncertainty.I would the Katerina Kosta's work, a "piano symbol" performance guidance resulted in sound is not always a soft. Her journal article also analyze this problem, and her ML model is better learn about the performer style instead of some kind of audio-to-loudness correspondence.

Same finding in Kim’s work utilizing LLMs for midi-velocity-to-dynamic  translation

actual_reply_item_table.reviewer_comment_exact: Section 3.1: This work is mentioned as the “most controlled” in the thesis; however predicting dynamics from a score in the absence of any dynamics markings or velocity info is a more unconstrained problem than dynamics prediction given input audio (where dynamics are present).

actual_reply_item_table.reviewer_comment_exact: Section 3.1 and beyond: to what extent should MIDI Velocity completion be style-specific or composer-specific?
actual_reply_item_table.relevant_exact_excerpt: So we changed our idea from " style control", to make a model can generalize to more data in different style.
actual_reply_item_table.assessment_zh: 过去从style control转向共享泛化模型；不是本次文稿决定。

reply_sources.native_exact_quote:
That's a great question, During my Dolby internship, we explored using style as a control parameter in a generative system. Composer could also be used as a coarse style label, for example “Chopin style” or “Beethoven style.”
However, we were facing the data limitation, we don't have enough training data for composer/style control. So we changed our idea from " style control", to make a model can generalize to more data in different style. 
You can see our human listening test analyse the "most-seen composer / unseen composer style" in train data, it exist a gap, but work well across those scenario.s.

actual_reply_item_table.reviewer_comment_exact: Section 3.2 and beyond considers the proposed work as “image-based”. Although there are some related figures with varying colours included in this chapter, I do not see any strong argument for using this term – the methodology does not treat dynamics as a colour channel or similar.
actual_reply_item_table.relevant_exact_excerpt: I would say the “image-like” is more proper. I will make revision.
actual_reply_item_table.assessment_zh: 明确澄清措辞并倾向image-like；未承诺改架构。

reply_sources.native_exact_quote:
Good question. The idea originally came from image-processing papers, especially the use of U-Net and window attention. We use “image-based” because both the input and output are two-dimensional pitch–time matrices, processed with two-dimensional convolutions.

The input is a binary piano roll, and the output is a single-channel velocity roll. We do not predict RGB colours. “Colourisation” is an analogy for adding velocity values to the existing note structure, it's good for general audiance understand, but I agree that the wording needs clarification.

I would say the “image-like” is more proper. I will make revision.

The degradation after Diff-Synth adaptation is consistent with acoustic mismatch, although we have not separately measured reconstruction fidelity and velocity-gradient accuracy on our target data.

reply_sources.native_exact_quote: We chose Huber because it provides smoother gradients for small PHE/OSF errors while retaining an L1-like penalty for large errors. We use β = 1, but we have not established that it performs better than MAE through a dedicated comparison.We will add more details about this in the thesis, thanks for rasing it.

VeloEst acts as the shared front-end of the framework, estimating note-wise MIDI velocities $\hat{V}$ from the performance audio and aligned note events. We use the score-informed HPT model with onset and frame as score-guidance, which is identified as the best VeloEst configuration in Chapter~\ref{ch:scoreinf}~\cite{he2026score}. We keep its architecture unchanged and use the publicly available checkpoint trained on MAESTRO with ground-truth velocity supervision $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{velo}}$. This fixed estimator keeps the cross-instrument experiment focused on the supervision interface rather than on introducing a new velocity-estimation architecture.
text_keyword_hits.authority: not an author revision decision; manuscript/method statement

text_keyword_hits.quote: The second method contribution introduces performance audio while keeping the note structure fixed through an aligned score. Chapter~\ref{ch:scoreinf} proposes a modular correction strategy: keep the AMT backbone unchanged, then use score information as a late residual correction signal for note-level velocity. This design is deliberately different from early-fusion score-informed transcription. It treats score information as a structural prior rather than as a replacement for acoustic evidence.
text_keyword_hits.authority: not an author revision decision; manuscript/method statement

text_keyword_hits.quote: The interface of the proposed system is intentionally simple. The AMT backbone first predicts a preliminary velocity map from audio. The aligned score is then converted into symbolic features at the same time resolution. A lightweight score-informed module finally corrects the preliminary estimate at note onsets. This design has three practical advantages. First, it keeps the acoustic front end reusable. Second, it allows the correction module to be attached to several AMT backbones with only small engineering changes. Third, it constrains the score-informed stage to a narrow task. The module adjusts \emph{how loudly} a note is played. It does not decide \emph{whether} the note exists.
text_keyword_hits.authority: not an author revision decision; manuscript/method statement

text_keyword_hits.quote: The main finding of this chapter is that score information is most useful when it is treated as a structural prior rather than as a full replacement for the acoustic model. The AMT backbone still supplies the initial estimate of performance intensity. The score-informed module only performs a targeted correction at onset locations. This division of labour keeps the system lightweight and explains why the gain transfers across backbones. It also clarifies why score information helps cross-dataset behaviour. The score does not change with microphone placement, room acoustics, or recording chain. It regularises a prediction target that is otherwise acoustically fragile.
text_keyword_hits.authority: not an author revision decision; manuscript/method statement

text_keyword_hits.quote: This chapter moved from symbolic completion to score-informed audio refinement. The task is still note-level MIDI velocity, but the estimate now starts from an AMT velocity branch and is corrected using aligned score structure. The proposed Transformer correction module deliberately sits late in the pipeline: it does not redesign the acoustic encoder, and it does not decide which notes exist. It only adjusts the velocity attached to known score onsets.
